pr_description:
## Summary

The `fd_renumber` syscall implementation had a subtle accounting bug that could corrupt the internal file descriptor tracking state and cause a host panic.

The `Descriptors` structure tracks open file descriptors in a `used` BTreeMap and a `free` list of available FD numbers to reuse. Previously, the `remove()` helper removed an FD from `used` and pushed it onto the `free` Vec. The `fd_renumber` implementation called `remove(from)` and then unconditionally inserted the descriptor at `to`.

This caused two corruption scenarios:

1. **Identity renumber (`from == to`)**: The FD was removed from `used` and added to `free`, then immediately re-inserted into `used`. The FD now exists in both `used` and `free` simultaneously.

2. **Renumber to a previously-closed FD**: If `to` was already on the `free` list (from a prior `fd_close`), inserting into `used` did not remove it from `free`. Again, the FD existed in both structures.

In either case, the next call to `push()` (e.g. from `path_open`) would pop the poisoned FD from `free`, then call `assert!(self.used.insert(fd, desc).is_none())`. Since the FD was already present in `used`, the insert returned `Some(...)`, triggering an unconditional panic — a guest-triggered host denial of service.

## Changes

- Changed `free` from `Vec<u32>` to `BTreeSet<u32>`, eliminating the possibility of duplicate entries
- Removed the `Deref`/`DerefMut` impls on `Descriptors` (which obscured direct `used` map access) and updated all call sites to explicitly use `.used.get()`, `.used.insert()`, etc.
- Replaced the `remove()` helper with inlined removal logic in `fd_close`, making the accounting explicit
- Rewrote `fd_renumber` to: (a) return `EBADF` if `from` is not open, (b) skip all mutation when `from == to`, and (c) explicitly remove `to` from `free` before inserting into `used` when renumbering to a previously-freed FD
- Updated `push()` to use `pop_last()` on the BTreeSet

## Test plan

- [ ] Existing preview1 fd_renumber tests pass
- [ ] `fd_renumber(n, n)` no longer corrupts FD state
- [ ] After `fd_renumber(fd, u32::MAX)`, subsequent `path_open` returns a valid FD without panicking
- [ ] `fd_close` correctly populates the free set so FD numbers are reused safely

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability is a data race in safe Rust: `Memory::_new` (called by both `Memory::new` and `Memory::new_async`) accepted any `MemoryType` without checking `ty.is_shared()`. Because `wasmtime::Memory` exposes safe byte-slice accessors (`data`, `data_mut`, `read`, `write`) that are not atomic, wrapping a WebAssembly shared linear memory in a `Memory` object allowed a second thread to concurrently mutate those bytes through the `SharedMemory` API, violating Rust's aliasing rules without any `unsafe` block in user code. The fix adds `if ty.is_shared() { bail!(...) }` at the top of `Memory::_new`, ensuring shared memory types are rejected and callers are directed to `SharedMemory::new` instead. This is the only change needed in this version of the codebase because the export/dispatch logic already correctly routes shared-memory exports to `SharedMemory` (via the `m.memory.memory.shared` flag check in `Extern::from_wasmtime_export`), and there is no coredump feature in this older codebase that also needs patching.
commit_message:
[Merged] Add shared memories (#4187)

* Add shared memories

This change adds the ability to use shared memories in Wasmtime when the
[threads proposal] is enabled. Shared memories are annotated as `shared`
in the WebAssembly syntax, e.g., `(memory 1 1 shared)`, and are
protected from concurrent access during `memory.size` and `memory.grow`.

[threads proposal]: https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads/blob/master/proposals/threads/Overview.md

In order to implement this in Wasmtime, there are two main cases to
cover:
    - a program may simply create a shared memory and possibly export it;
    this means that Wasmtime itself must be able to create shared
    memories
    - a user may create a shared memory externally and pass it in as an
    import during instantiation; this is the case when the program
    contains code like `(import "env" "memory" (memory 1 1
    shared))`--this case is handled by a new Wasmtime API
    type--`SharedMemory`

Because of the first case, this change allows any of the current
memory-creation mechanisms to work as-is. Wasmtime can still create
either static or dynamic memories in either on-demand or pooling modes,
and any of these memories can be considered shared. When shared, the
`Memory` runtime container will lock appropriately during `memory.size`
and `memory.grow` operations; since all memories use this container, it
is an ideal place for implementing the locking once and once only.

The second case is covered by the new `SharedMemory` structure. It uses
the same `Mmap` allocation under the hood as non-shared memories, but
allows the user to perform the allocation externally to Wasmtime and
share the memory across threads (via an `Arc`). The pointer address to
the actual memory is carefully wired through and owned by the
`SharedMemory` structure itself. This means that there are differing
views of where to access the pointer (i.e., `VMMemoryDefinition`): for
owned memories (the default), the `VMMemoryDefinition` is stored
directly by the `VMContext`; in the `SharedMemory` case, however, this
`VMContext` must point to this separate structure.

To ensure that the `VMContext` can always point to the correct
`VMMemoryDefinition`, this change alters the `VMContext` structure.
Since a `SharedMemory` owns its own `VMMemoryDefinition`, the
`defined_memories` table in the `VMContext` becomes a sequence of
pointers--in the shared memory case, they point to the
`VMMemoryDefinition` owned by the `SharedMemory` and in the owned memory
case (i.e., not shared) they point to `VMMemoryDefinition`s stored in a
new table, `owned_memories`.

This change adds an additional indirection (through the `*mut
VMMemoryDefinition` pointer) that could add overhead. Using an imported
memory as a proxy, we measured a 1-3% overhead of this approach on the
`pulldown-cmark` benchmark. To avoid this, Cranelift-generated code will
special-case the owned memory access (i.e., load a pointer directly to
the `owned_memories` entry) for `memory.size` so that only
shared memories (and imported memories, as before) incur the indirection
cost.

fix_commit_message:
Prevent using shared memories with `Memory` (#12022)

* Prevent using shared memories with `Memory`

This commit fixes a few issues where it was possible to represent a wasm
shared linear memory with the `wasmtime::Memory` type. This is not sound
because `wasmtime::Memory` provides safe Rust access to the bytes where
that is not possible with wasm shared memories. Shared memories in Rust
must be represented by `SharedMemory`, not `wasmtime::Memory`.

Specifically this commit prevents two vectors of this happening:

1. `Memory::new` now requires that the memory type specified is
   non-shared. Instead `SharedMemory::new` must be used instead.

2. Core dumps now skip over shared memories when iterating over all
   memories in the store. Supporting shared memories is left to a future
   feature request for now.

* CI fixes

findings.message: The `Memory::_new` helper (called by both `Memory::new` and `Memory::new_async`) accepts any `MemoryType`, including shared memories, without checking `ty.is_shared()`. Because `wasmtime::Memory` exposes safe Rust methods that return `&[u8]` slices (e.g., `Memory::data`), allowing it to wrap a WebAssembly shared linear memory is unsound: another thread may concurrently write to the same bytes through the `SharedMemory` API, creating a data race in safe Rust code. The fix adds `if ty.is_shared() { bail!(...) }` at the entry of `_new`. Additionally, the core-dump path (`WasmCoreDump::new`) collected all store memories as `Vec<Memory>` without filtering out shared ones, exposing shared memory bytes via the unsynchronised `Memory::data` API during crash capture.
findings.suggestion: Add a guard at the top of `Memory::_new` (or equivalently in `Memory::new`) that rejects shared `MemoryType` values: `if ty.is_shared() { bail!("shared memories must be created through `SharedMemory`") }`. In `WasmCoreDump::new`, filter out shared memories before collecting them into `store_memories`: `store_memories.retain(|m| !m.wasmtime_ty(store).shared);`

ground_truth.root_cause: When shared memory support was introduced in commit 2b52f47b83 ('Add shared memories'), the `Memory::new` / `Memory::_new` code path was not updated to guard against shared `MemoryType` arguments. The assumption baked into `wasmtime::Memory`'s safe API — that no concurrent mutations occur — was silently violated when a caller passed `MemoryType::shared(...)` to `Memory::new`.

pr_description:
* Add shared memories

This change adds the ability to use shared memories in Wasmtime when the
[threads proposal] is enabled. Shared memories are annotated as `shared`
in the WebAssembly syntax, e.g., `(memory 1 1 shared)`, and are
protected from concurrent access during `memory.size` and `memory.grow`.

[threads proposal]: https://github.com/WebAssembly/threads/blob/master/proposals/threads/Overview.md

In order to implement this in Wasmtime, there are two main cases to
cover:
    - a program may simply create a shared memory and possibly export it;
    this means that Wasmtime itself must be able to create shared
    memories
    - a user may create a shared memory externally and pass it in as an
    import during instantiation; this is the case when the program
    contains code like `(import "env" "memory" (memory 1 1
    shared))`--this case is handled by a new Wasmtime API
    type--`SharedMemory`

Because of the first case, this change allows any of the current
memory-creation mechanisms to work as-is. Wasmtime can still create
either static or dynamic memories in either on-demand or pooling modes,
and any of these memories can be considered shared. When shared, the
`Memory` runtime container will lock appropriately during `memory.size`
and `memory.grow` operations; since all memories use this container, it
is an ideal place for implementing the locking once and once only.

The second case is covered by the new `SharedMemory` structure. It uses
the same `Mmap` allocation under the hood as non-shared memories, but
allows the user to perform the allocation externally to Wasmtime and
share the memory across threads (via an `Arc`). The pointer address to
the actual memory is carefully wired through and owned by the
`SharedMemory` structure itself. This means that there are differing
views of where to access the pointer (i.e., `VMMemoryDefinition`): for
owned memories (the default), the `VMMemoryDefinition` is stored
directly by the `VMContext`; in the `SharedMemory` case, however, this
`VMContext` must point to this separate structure.

To ensure that the `VMContext` can always point to the correct
`VMMemoryDefinition`, this change alters the `VMContext` structure.
Since a `SharedMemory` owns its own `VMMemoryDefinition`, the
`defined_memories` table in the `VMContext` becomes a sequence of
pointers--in the shared memory case, they point to the
`VMMemoryDefinition` owned by the `SharedMemory` and in the owned memory
case (i.e., not shared) they point to `VMMemoryDefinition`s stored in a
new table, `owned_memories`.

This change adds an additional indirection (through the `*mut
VMMemoryDefinition` pointer) that could add overhead. Using an imported
memory as a proxy, we measured a 1-3% overhead of this approach on the
`pulldown-cmark` benchmark. To avoid this, Cranelift-generated code will
special-case the owned memory access (i.e., load a pointer directly to
the `owned_memories` entry) for `memory.size` so that only
shared memories (and imported memories, as before) incur the indirection
cost.

agent_reasoning: The bug was that the ISLE `fcopysign` lowering rules for x64 passed operands `a` and `b` directly to vector bitwise AND instructions (ANDPS/ANDPD) without first forcing them into XMM registers. Cranelift's load-sinking pass would then fold a scalar `f32.load` or `f64.load` directly into the vector instruction's memory operand, but those instructions only have a 128-bit memory form — not 32-bit or 64-bit — so the emitted code performed an unintended 128-bit (16-byte) memory read instead of a 4-byte or 8-byte read. Near the end of a valid memory region this could read into unmapped memory (crashing the host) or out-of-sandbox data. The fix adds explicit `(a Xmm a)` and `(b Xmm b)` bindings at the top of each rule, ensuring operands are materialized into registers before being used in vector AND instructions, which prevents load-sinking from widening the load to 128 bits.

fix_commit_message:
Cranelift: x64: fix incorrect load-sinking in `copysign` operator. (#12435)

* Cranelift: x64: do not incorrectly widen loads sunk into `fcopysign`.

The implementation of the `fcopysign` operator uses vector bitwise AND
instructions on the floating-point/vector registers containing the
inputs to the operator. This is a reasonable implementation as the
instruction set does not have scalar (single-lane) bitwise
operators. However, when load-sinking automatically kicks in for an
operand to an `andps`, it can turn a 64-bit load (`f64.load`) into a
128-bit load incorrectly.

This load-widening can cause out-of-bounds accesses where they were
not expected. When dynamic bounds checks are enabled, we compile
assuming the correct load-operator width is codegen'd; a too-wide load
could read beyond the checked bound, either into unmapped
memory (crashing the process) or, worse, valid data outside the
sandbox. In the case of `fcopysign` the result of that read is not
directly available, because it will go into the high (unused)
lane, but the out-of-bounds read itself is a problem.

Thanks to louismerlin for reporting!

* Re-bless Cranelift filetests.

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

intro_commit_message:
x64: Lower fcopysign, ceil, floor, nearest, and trunc in ISLE (#4730)

https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/pull/4730
pr_description:
## Summary

The ISLE lowering rules for `fcopysign` on x64 use vector bitwise AND instructions (`ANDPS`/`ANDPD`, `ANDNPS`/`ANDNPD`) to manipulate the sign bit of floating-point values. These vector instructions operate on 128-bit XMM registers.

Previously, the operands `a` and `b` were passed directly to the vector AND instructions without first being materialized into XMM registers. Cranelift's load-sinking optimization can transparently fold a memory load into an instruction's memory operand. When the operand came from a scalar `f32.load` or `f64.load`, load-sinking would fold the load directly into the `ANDPS`/`ANDPD` instruction's memory operand slot. Because those vector instructions have no scalar (32-bit or 64-bit) memory form — only 128-bit — this caused the emitted code to perform a 128-bit (16-byte) memory read instead of the intended 32-bit or 64-bit load.

This widened load can read up to 12 or 8 extra bytes beyond the intended boundary, which can:
- Cause an out-of-bounds read into guard pages (DoS via segfault / process abort), or
- Read data outside the wasm linear memory sandbox when guard pages are disabled.

## Fix

Force operands `a` and `b` into XMM registers explicitly at the start of each `fcopysign` ISLE rule by binding them with `(a Xmm a)` and `(b Xmm b)`. This prevents load-sinking from widening a scalar load to 128 bits, since the operand will already reside in a register by the time the AND instructions are emitted.

## Test plan

- [ ] Existing filetest `cranelift/filetests/filetests/isa/x64/simd-bitwise-avx.clif` updated to reflect that `fcopysign` with a loaded operand now emits an explicit scalar `vmovss`/`vmovsd` rather than folding the load into `vandps`/`vandpd`.
- [ ] Run `cargo test -p cranelift-codegen` to verify no regressions.
- [ ] Confirm that the generated assembly for `fcopysign` with a memory operand uses a scalar load instruction followed by a register-form AND instruction.
pr_title: Cranelift: x64: force `fcopysign` operands into registers to prevent incorrect load-sinking

location.snippet:
(rule (lower (has_type $F64 (fcopysign a @ (value_type $F64) b)))
      (let ((sign_bit Xmm (imm $F64 0x8000000000000000)))
        (x64_orpd
          (x64_andnpd sign_bit a)
          (x64_andpd sign_bit b))))

findings.message: The ISLE lowering rules for `fcopysign` (both F32 and F64 variants) pass operands `a` and `b` directly to vector bitwise AND instructions (`x64_andps`/`x64_andnps` for F32, `x64_andpd`/`x64_andnpd` for F64) without first forcing them into XMM registers. Cranelift's load-sinking pass can then transparently fold a memory load (e.g., from `f64.load`) directly into these vector AND instructions as a memory operand. Because these vector instructions (`ANDPS`/`ANDPD`) operate on 128-bit XMM operands, a memory form of the instruction performs a 128-bit (16-byte) load instead of the expected 64-bit (8-byte) load for F64 or 32-bit (4-byte) load for F32. When the wasm linear memory address is near the end of a valid region, this widened load can extend 8 bytes beyond the checked bound — into unmapped guard pages (causing a segfault) or, with guard pages disabled, into out-of-sandbox data. With signals-based-traps disabled and guard pages enabled, the segfault is uncaught and aborts the host process (DoS).
findings.suggestion: Force operands `a` and `b` into XMM registers before using them as operands to vector AND instructions, so load-sinking cannot widen a scalar (32/64-bit) load into a 128-bit vector memory operand. Add explicit register bindings `(a Xmm a)` and `(b Xmm b)` in the `let` block before passing them to `x64_andps`/`x64_andpd` etc.
findings.suggestion_code:
(rule (lower (has_type $F64 (fcopysign a @ (value_type $F64) b)))
      (let ((sign_bit Xmm (imm $F64 0x8000000000000000))
            (a Xmm a) ;; force into reg so we don't sink a 128-bit load.
            (b Xmm b))
        (x64_orpd
          (x64_andnpd sign_bit a)
          (x64_andpd sign_bit b))))
findings.title: Incorrect 128-bit load widening in fcopysign ISLE lowering rules

fix_commit.author: Chris Fallin
fix_commit.message: Cranelift: x64: fix incorrect load-sinking in `copysign` operator. (#12435)

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Incorrect 128-bit load widening in fcopysign ISLE lowering rules
Related location for: Incorrect 128-bit load widening in fcopysign ISLE lowering rules

ground_truth.root_cause: The ISLE `fcopysign` lowering rules for x64 do not materialize operands into registers before using them in vector AND operations. Cranelift's generic load-sinking optimization then folds a scalar load directly into the ANDPD/ANDPS instruction's memory operand slot. Because those instructions have no scalar (64-bit or 32-bit) memory form — only 128-bit — the result is an unintended 128-bit memory read, reading 8 extra bytes beyond the intended load boundary.

pr_description: https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/pull/4730
pr_title: x64: Lower fcopysign, ceil, floor, nearest, and trunc in ISLE (#4730)

agent_reasoning: The bug is in the ISLE rule for `f64x2.splat` fallback (no SSE3): `(rule 0 (lower (has_type $F64X2 (splat src))) (x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00))`. By passing `src` directly, Cranelift's load-sinking can fold an f64.load into the pshufd memory operand. Since pshufd reads 128 bits (16 bytes) but the original load is only 64 bits (8 bytes), this causes an out-of-bounds read of up to 8 extra bytes past the intended address. The fix wraps `src` with `(put_in_xmm src)`, which forces the value into an XMM register first, blocking load-sinking and ensuring pshufd only ever uses a register operand in this path.

intro_commit_message:
x64: Avoid using `movddup` without SSSE3 (#6496)

* x64: Avoid using `movddup` without SSSE3

Update the lowerings for 64-bit splats to use `pshufd` instead, as LLVM
does.

* Disable runtest for now
pr_description:
When lowering `f64x2.splat` on x86-64 without SSE3, the fallback rule uses `pshufd` to broadcast the lower 64-bit lane to the upper lane. Previously, the source value was passed directly to `x64_pshufd`, which allowed Cranelift's load-sinking mechanism to fold a sinkable `f64.load` directly into the `pshufd` memory operand.

The problem is that `pshufd` is a 128-bit instruction and always reads 16 bytes from memory, but an `f64.load` only intends to read 8 bytes. Sinking the load into `pshufd` therefore causes an over-read of 8 extra bytes beyond the intended load address.

This change wraps the source operand with `put_in_xmm`, which forces the value to be materialized into an XMM register before being passed to `pshufd`. This prevents load-sinking from folding the 8-byte load into the 16-byte `pshufd` memory operand, ensuring the instruction only ever reads from an XMM register operand (not memory) in the non-SSE3 fallback path.

The SSE3 path (`movddup`) is unaffected — it is a 64-bit load-and-broadcast instruction and correctly reads only 8 bytes.
pr_title: x64: Fix `f64x2.splat` load sinking into `pshufd`

findings.message: In the ISLE lowering for `f64x2.splat` on x86-64 without SSE3, the rule passes `src` directly to `x64_pshufd`. Cranelift's load-sinking mechanism can sink a sinkable memory load into the `pshufd` instruction operand. However, `pshufd` always reads 128 bits (16 bytes) from memory, whereas the original `f64.load` only reads 64 bits (8 bytes). This means the lowering reads up to 8 extra bytes past the intended load address. Depending on Wasmtime configuration: (1) with guard pages disabled, out-of-sandbox data is read into the upper bits of an XMM register (data not visible to WebAssembly but still an unintended read); (2) with guard pages enabled and signals-based-traps enabled, the widened load hits a guard page causing a segfault caught as a WebAssembly trap (incorrect behavior but not a security issue); (3) with guard pages enabled and signals-based-traps disabled, the segfault is uncaught and terminates the host process (DoS).
findings.suggestion: Force the source operand into an XMM register via `put_in_xmm` before passing it to `x64_pshufd`. This prevents Cranelift's load-sinking from widening the load from 8 bytes to 16 bytes. The fix is to change `(x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00)` to `(x64_pshufd (put_in_xmm src) 0b01_00_01_00)`.

ground_truth.root_cause: The ISLE rule `(rule 0 (lower (has_type $F64X2 (splat src))) (x64_pshufd src 0b01_00_01_00))` was introduced in commit 8c530771 as a fallback for `movddup` (SSE3) on processors without SSE3 support. By passing `src` directly (rather than via `put_in_xmm`), the rule allows Cranelift's load-sinking to fold a `f64.load` into the `pshufd` memory operand. The `pshufd` instruction, however, is a 128-bit instruction and always reads 16 bytes from memory—twice as many bytes as intended for an 8-byte float load. The sinkable-load specialization rule (rule 5/6) for this case uses `movddup` gated on `has_sse3`/`use_ssse3`, but on SSE3-less hosts the rule 0 fallback takes effect without any guard preventing load sinking.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix f89d910b4a24 on top of intro 7f781b86e531 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): After PR #11254 updated the `table_fill_func_ref` and `table_fill_gc_ref` libcall intrinsics to accept a `DefinedTableIndex` (the index into only defined/non-imported tables), the corresponding Winch code path in `visit_table_fill` was not updated. Winch continued to insert the raw `table` u32 value (a module-level `TableIndex`) directly onto the argument stack. When a wasm module contains imported tables, `TableIndex` and `DefinedTableIndex` occupy different index spaces. Passing a module-level index where a defined-table index is expected causes `get_defined_table` to access an out-of-bounds slot, triggering a host panic. Additionally, even without an out-of-bounds access, the mismatch can silently operate on the wrong table. Root cause: PR #11254 changed the calling convention of `table_fill_func_ref` and `table_fill_gc_ref` libcalls from `TableIndex` to `DefinedTableIndex` in both Cranelift codegen and the runtime libcall implementations, but the corresponding Winch code path (`visit_table_fill` in `winch/codegen/src/visitor.rs`) was not updated. The existing helper `prepare_builtin_defined_table_arg` already existed and was used for other table instructions (e.g., `table_grow`), but was overlooked for `table.fill`.
commit_message:
[Merged] Update `table.fill` intrinsics to use defined indices (#11254)

Similar to previous refactorings which handles the imported/exported
distinction in wasm instead of in host code this updates the
`table.fill`-related libcall intrinsics to take a defined table index
instead of a general table index, enabling using a currently-safer
helper function.
fix_commit_message:
winch: Fix a host panic when executing `table.fill` (#13010)

This commit fixes a possible panic when a Winch-compiled module executes
the `table.fill` instruction. Refactoring in #11254 updated Cranelift
but forgot to update Winch meaning that Winch's indices were still using
the module-level indices instead of the `DefinedTableIndex` space. This
adds some tests and updates Winch's translation to use preexisting
helpers.

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

commit_message:
Update `table.fill` intrinsics to use defined indices (#11254)

Similar to previous refactorings which handles the imported/exported
distinction in wasm instead of in host code this updates the
`table.fill`-related libcall intrinsics to take a defined table index
instead of a general table index, enabling using a currently-safer
helper function.

findings.message: After PR #11254 updated the `table_fill_func_ref` and `table_fill_gc_ref` libcall intrinsics to accept a `DefinedTableIndex` (the index into only defined/non-imported tables), the corresponding Winch code path in `visit_table_fill` was not updated. Winch continued to insert the raw `table` u32 value (a module-level `TableIndex`) directly onto the argument stack. When a wasm module contains imported tables, `TableIndex` and `DefinedTableIndex` occupy different index spaces. Passing a module-level index where a defined-table index is expected causes `get_defined_table` to access an out-of-bounds slot, triggering a host panic. Additionally, even without an out-of-bounds access, the mismatch can silently operate on the wrong table.
findings.suggestion: Replace direct insertion of the raw `table` u32 with a call to `prepare_builtin_defined_table_arg(table_index, at, builtin)`, which correctly converts the module-level `TableIndex` to a `DefinedTableIndex` (and resolves the owning vmctx for imported tables), consistent with how `visit_table_grow` and `visit_table_size` handle this.

let callee = self.prepare_builtin_defined_table_arg(table_index, at, builtin)?;
FnCall::emit::<M>(&mut self.env, self.masm, &mut self.context, callee)?;

agent_reasoning: The vulnerability arises from calling `shift_masked_imm ty n` with the memory-access type (`ty`) rather than the type of the `ishl` expression. When these types differ in bit-width (e.g., load type is i32 but the index shift is i64), the masking is wrong. For instance, shift amount 34 with load type i32 gives `34 & 31 = 2`, satisfying the `4 == 1 << 2` guard and causing the code generator to emit an AArch64 `RegScaled` instruction with LSL #2. But the correct CLIF semantics perform a 34-bit shift, which should not be folded into a RegScaled addressing mode at all. With a carefully chosen index value (e.g., 2^30), this produces an out-of-bounds memory access that bypasses sandbox bounds checks — a sandbox escape. The fix captures the `ishl` type as `shift_ty` and passes it to `shift_masked_imm`, ensuring the guard uses the correct bit-width mask.

intro_commit_message:
aarch64: Fix an overflowing shift panic (#10382)

Ensure that a compile-time-shift-amount is masked to avoid a debug
assertion about an overflowing shift.

Closes #10373
pr_description:
When folding an `iadd` + `ishl` pair into a `RegScaled` addressing mode on AArch64, the shift amount must be validated against the type of the `ishl` instruction — not the type of the surrounding memory access (load/store).

Previously, `shift_masked_imm` was called with `ty` (the load/store type), which caused incorrect shift-amount masking when the index shift type differs from the access type. For example, with a `load.i32` and an `ishl.i64` by 34, the old code computed `shift_masked_imm(I32, 34) = 34 & 31 = 2`, making the guard condition `4 == 1 << 2` pass. This erroneously generates a `RegScaled` addressing mode with LSL #2, while the correct CLIF semantics call for a shift of 34 — which should not fold at all.

This PR introduces `shift_ty` as a type binding on the `ishl` pattern in rules 6 and 7, so that `shift_masked_imm shift_ty n` uses the actual type of the shift operand. The guard then correctly computes `shift_masked_imm(I64, 34) = 34`, making the condition `4 == 1 << 34` (false), preventing the invalid fold.

findings.message: In `amode_no_more_iconst` rules 6 and 7 (ISLE lowering for AArch64 address-mode selection), the condition `(if-let true (u64_eq (ty_bytes ty) (u64_shl 1 (shift_masked_imm ty n))))` calls `shift_masked_imm` with `ty` — the type of the memory access (load/store) — rather than the type of the `ishl` value `y`. The `shift_masked_imm` function masks the shift amount `n` to the bit-width of the provided type (e.g., `n & 31` for i32, `n & 63` for i64). When `ty` (the load type, e.g. i32) has fewer bits than the shift operand's type (e.g. i64 for 64-bit WebAssembly memory indices), the mask is incorrect. For example, with load type i32 and shift-value type i64, `n = 34` produces `shift_masked_imm(i32, 34) = 34 & 31 = 2`, making the condition `4 == 1 << 2 = 4` pass. This erroneously generates a `RegScaled` addressing mode with shift 2, whereas the correct CLIF semantics of `ishl.i64 index 34` are a shift of 34. When `index = 2^30`, the CLIF semantics compute `index << 34 = 2^64 ≡ 0 (mod 2^64)`, so the explicit bounds check sees address = base + 0 (passes). But the emitted `LDR [base, index, LSL #2]` instruction computes `base + index * 4 = base + 4 GB`, escaping the sandbox.

This ensures the shift amount is masked according to the shift value's bit-width (the correct WebAssembly/Cranelift semantics for ishl) rather than the load's type width. Also change `u64_shl` to `u64_wrapping_shl` to avoid overflow.

ground_truth.root_cause: Commit ba1e663bac ('aarch64: Fix an overflowing shift panic') introduced `shift_masked_imm ty n` in rules 6 and 7 to mask the shift amount before comparing it to `log2(ty_bytes)`. However, `ty` here is the type of the memory access (load/store), whereas the shift amount's effective mask must come from the type of the `ishl` value (the index register). When these two types differ in bit-width — as is common in 64-bit WebAssembly where the memory index is i64 but the loaded element size gives a smaller `ty` like i32 — the wrong mask enables false matches: e.g., `shift_masked_imm(i32, 34) = 2` makes the check `4 == 1 << 2` pass, but the correct `shift_masked_imm(i64, 34) = 34` would give `4 == 1 << 34` (false). The generated RegScaled AArch64 instruction then encodes the shift as `log2(ty_bytes) = 2`, diverging from the CLIF-level shift of 34.

Vulnerability (UseAfterFree): The `StringPool` struct uses an unsafe lifetime transmutation to store `&'static str` keys in its `map` field that actually point into the memory owned by its own `strings` field. The `TryClone` implementation naively clones both fields independently: `self.map.try_clone()` copies the HashMap, which copies those raw `&'static str` keys (still pointing at the ORIGINAL pool's string allocation), while `self.strings.try_clone()` allocates a fresh, separate copy of the string data. The resulting clone therefore holds a `map` whose keys dangle into the original pool's allocation. Once the original `StringPool` (and thus the original `wasmtime::Linker`) is dropped and its `strings` are deallocated, any lookup through the clone's map accesses freed memory — a classic use-after-free. The fix re-interns every string through the new pool's `insert()` so the cloned map's keys point into the clone's own `strings` allocation. Root cause: The `StringPool` struct deliberately uses `unsafe { mem::transmute::<&str, &'static str>(...) }` to launder borrows of its own `strings` field so they can serve as HashMap keys. This internal invariant — that the 'static keys are actually self-referential borrows — is invisible to the derived/generic `TryClone` machinery. Cloning the map field copies these raw pointers as-is, without relocating them to point into the new clone's storage, breaking the invariant in the copy.

agent_reasoning: The buggy code used `ty.can_elide_bounds_check(tunables, host_page_size_log2)` to decide whether to call `set_protection` when shrinking an accessible region back to its initial size. This predicate is too conservative: when `memory_guard_size == 0` and `memory_reservation < 4GiB` with `max_memory_size == memory_reservation`, `can_use_virtual_memory` returns true (the compiler assumes virtual-memory semantics) but `can_elide_bounds_check` returns false. As a result the pooling allocator would skip the `set_protection` call and leave previously mapped pages readable/writable, allowing a newly spawned Wasm instance to read linear-memory contents from a prior instance — a sandbox escape. The fix replaces the predicate with `ty.can_use_virtual_memory(...)`, which correctly captures exactly the cases where memory protections must be reset.

pr_description:
When the pooling allocator resets a linear memory slot for reuse, it must revoke memory protections on any pages that were accessible beyond the initial size. The condition guarding `set_protection` previously checked `ty.can_elide_bounds_check(tunables, host_page_size_log2)` as the fallback predicate, but this is too conservative: it returns `false` when there are no guard pages even if the memory reservation is large enough for the compiler to assume virtual-memory semantics for out-of-bounds accesses.

The correct predicate is `ty.can_use_virtual_memory(tunables, host_page_size_log2)`, which returns `true` whenever the compiler relies on virtual-memory semantics regardless of guard-page size. Using this predicate ensures that previously mapped pages are always de-protected before a new Wasm instance is placed into the slot, regardless of the specific combination of `memory_guard_size`, `memory_reservation`, and `max_memory_size` tunables in effect.

This change affects `MemoryImageSlot::assign_init_image` in `crates/wasmtime/src/runtime/vm/cow.rs`.

The reset of VM permissions must happen whenever virtual memory semantics are relied upon by the compiler, not only when bounds checks can be fully elided. agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix db7fb47b8e14 on top of intro bb5e4bbaf9a6 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): Wasmtime's Winch baseline (single-pass) compiler computes an `OperandSize` for each kind of Wasm load via `LoadKind::derive_operand_size()`. This size is used both to emit the machine-code load and, critically, to perform/encode the linear-memory bounds/guard check for the access. The January 2025 `wasm_load` simplification refactor (PR #10012) introduced `operand_size_for_vector()`, which derived a size of 1, 2, or 4 bytes for the SIMD 'vector extend' load variants (`v128.load8x8_{s,u}`, `v128.load16x4_{s,u}`, `v128.load32x2_{s,u}`) based on the *source lane width* rather than the *total bytes actually read*. All of these instructions read a full 8 bytes (64 bits) of linear memory and widen each lane, so the derived size undercounted the real access footprint by a factor of 2x-8x. PR #10127 fixed this by hard-coding `OperandSize::S64` for all `VectorExtendKind` variants. Root cause: The refactor in #10012 conflated 'bits per source lane before widening' with 'total bytes read from memory' when deriving the OperandSize for vector-extend loads. The derived size is reused for both bounds checking and instruction emission, so an incorrect (too-small) per-lane size was propagated into the memory-safety-relevant bounds computation instead of being independently fixed at 8 bytes (the true width of the SIMD extend-load instructions on x86-64/AArch64).
commit_message:
winch: Simplify the handling of `wasm_load`s (#10012)

This commit aims to simplify how `wasm_load`s are currently handled in
the compiler by reducing the number of invariants that need to be
encoded at callsites which make their emission error prone.

Concretely this change:

* Augments `ExtendKind`, to account for unsigned extends; prior to this
  commit it wasn't explicit which loads required unsigned extends.
* Derive `OperandSize` from `ExtendKind`, removing from the caller the
  responsibility of encoding the operand size to use.

winch: Simplify the handling of `wasm_load`s (#10012)

This commit aims to simplify how `wasm_load`s are currently handled in
the compiler by reducing the number of invariants that need to be
encoded at callsites which make their emission error prone.

Concretely this change:

* Augments `ExtendKind`, to account for unsigned extends; prior to this

* Derive `OperandSize` from `ExtendKind`, removing from the caller the
  responsibility of encoding the operand size to use.

findings.message: The Winch baseline compiler's `LoadKind::derive_operand_size()` computes the `OperandSize` that is passed down into `wasm_load`/`load_impl` to perform the Wasm linear-memory bounds check and emit the actual load instruction. For `LoadKind::VectorExtend(vector)` (used for v128 `load8x8`/`load16x4`/`load32x2` sign/zero-extending SIMD loads), this commit routes the size through the newly added `operand_size_for_vector()` helper, which maps V128Extend8x8{S,U} -> OperandSize::S8, V128Extend16x4{S,U} -> OperandSize::S16, and V128Extend32x2{S,U} -> OperandSize::S32. However, all of these Wasm vector-extend-load instructions actually read 8 bytes (64 bits) from linear memory before widening into 8/16/32-bit lanes of a v128 — e.g. `v128.load32x2_s` reads two 32-bit lanes (8 bytes total), not 4. Because the derived (too-small) OperandSize is what callers use both to size the actual memory access and to validate/bound the access against the heap/guard region, the bounds check and the code emitted for the load are checking/loading fewer bytes (1, 2, or 4) than are truly read (8), allowing the load to read up to 4-7 bytes past the validated/intended bound of linear memory for addresses near the end of the accessible region.
findings.suggestion: Derive the operand size for all `VectorExtendKind` variants as 64 bits (`OperandSize::S64`), since every v128 extend-load (load8x8/load16x4/load32x2, signed or unsigned) reads a full 8-byte quantity from linear memory regardless of the resulting narrow lane width. Remove the per-variant 8/16/32-bit mapping in `operand_size_for_vector` (or delete the helper entirely) and have `derive_operand_size` return `OperandSize::S64` directly for `Self::VectorExtend(_)`, matching how the actual load/bounds-check size is computed.

agent_reasoning: The intro commit added logic to capture the spawned task's error when the oneshot receiver signals a disconnect, using `task.await` and `.expect_err("if the receiver has an error, the task must have failed")`. This conflates two independent signals: the receiver erroring (sender dropped) and the task's own result being an `Err`. A guest component whose `handle` export returns `Ok(())` without ever calling `response-outparam::set` causes the sender to be dropped (so the receiver errors) while the task itself resolves to `Ok(())` — violating the assumption and causing `.expect_err` to panic, crashing the `wasmtime serve` process (a remotely triggerable DoS via a malicious or buggy guest component). The fix replaces the panicking `expect_err` with an explicit three-way match on the task's `Result` (`Ok(Ok(()))`, `Ok(Err(e))`, `Err(e)`), handling the "never called set but didn't error" case gracefully by reporting an error instead of panicking, and returns the error with added context instead of panicking.

findings.message: In `handle_request` in `src/commands/serve.rs`, when the `receiver` oneshot channel errors out (meaning the response-outparam `set` method was never invoked by the guest), the code awaits the spawned task and calls `.expect_err("if the receiver has an error, the task must have failed")` on its result. This assumes that if the guest never called `set`, the task must have returned an `Err`. However, a guest Wasm component can legitimately return `Ok(())` from its `handle` export without ever invoking `response-outparam::set` (e.g. it simply forgets to call it, or returns early without error). In that case `task.await` yields `Ok(Ok(()))`, so `r` is `Ok(())`, and `Result::expect_err` panics because the value is not an `Err`. Since this path is driven directly by externally-supplied/untrusted Wasm guest code processing an HTTP request in the `wasmtime serve` CLI command, any malicious or buggy guest component can deterministically crash the host process serving HTTP traffic, resulting in a remotely triggerable denial of service.
findings.suggestion: Do not assume the task must have returned an error when the receiver fails. Instead, explicitly handle the `Ok(Ok(()))` case (task completed successfully but never invoked `set`) by producing a dedicated error/bail instead of calling `.expect_err()`, which panics on that input. The actual fix (commit ad21d9581d) matches on `task.await` as `Ok(Ok(())) => bail!(...)`, `Ok(Err(e)) => e`, `Err(e) => e.into()`, avoiding the panicking `expect_err` call entirely.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 04eee2182605 on top of intro 0a29578f1095 via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (OutOfBoundsRead): When compiling allocation of a wasm GC `array` type whose element type is itself a GC reference (e.g. `(array (mut (ref null $other)))`), the DRC (deferred reference counting) GC compiler mis-computed the 'number of GC references' field stored in the object's common GC header. Instead of storing the element count (length) of the array, it stored the array's total allocation size in bytes (`base_size + len * elem_size`), reusing the `size` ir::Value that was meant only for the allocation-size argument to the raw allocator. Root cause: The commit that introduced transitive dec-ref tracing in the DRC collector (#10401) added a new `num_gc_refs` header field used to bound the slice of outgoing GC edges traced during collection. For arrays of GC-ref elements, the author intended to pass the array length but accidentally reused the `size` local (the array's byte size in memory, computed by `emit_array_size`), since both were available in scope and the mistake (size vs. len) was an easy one given they are used adjacently. There was no type-level distinction between a 'byte size' ir::Value and an 'element count' ir::Value, so the compiler could not catch the mismatch.
commit_message:
Transitively dec-ref objects in the DRC collector (#10401)

* Transitively dec-ref objects in the DRC collector

Previously, the DRC collector only performed shallow reference counting where if
an object's ref count was decremented and reached zero, then we would deallocate
that object, but we would not decrement the reference counts of any other object
that was referenced by it. This commit changes that, so that now we will
decrement the reference counts of other objects referenced by an object that is
being deallocated.

This requires some method of tracing an object's outgoing edges. To avoid
needing to keep around and dispatch upon type-specific information about which
struct fields are GC references, for example, we instead pack all GC references
at the start of the object, just after its header. We additionally keep a count
of how many GC references an object has in its header. This allows us to create
a slice of any object's GC references, and we can uniformly trace any GC
object's outgoing edges. We don't need to reflect on the GC object's actual
type.

A final detail: the DRC collector was previously storing the object size in the
common GC header's reserved bits. It now stores the number of GC refs there
instead, and the object size is stored in its own field in the DRC-specific
header, next to the ref count. This is nice because, since we are making the DRC
header larger anyways, it raises the DRC collector's implementation limit on
object size from `u27::MAX` to `u32::MAX`.

Fixes #9701

* update disas tests

* Remove newly-added debug-assert that isn't true in certain edge cases

Sometimes we need to deallocate uninitialized objects when initializing their
fields fails, and this assertion trips.

* fix some tests by returning an error of the correct kind of trap

rather than a generic anyhow error

* fix tracing GC refs on big-endian architectures

We can't cast to a slice, we need to do conversion from little-endian bytes.
fix_commit_message:
Fix a bug where arrays of GC refs were misreporting their count of GC edges (#10453)

* Fix a bug where arrays of GC refs were misreporting their count of GC edges

They were accidentally reporting the size of their GC reference elements, rather
than the count.

* fix miri ignore attr

ground_truth.reason: This PR includes the feature with the fix already applied, so the vulnerability is not present

findings.message: In `DrcCompiler::alloc_array` (crates/cranelift/src/gc/enabled/drc.rs), when allocating a `(array (ref ...))` whose elements are themselves GC references, the code computes `num_gc_refs` by reusing the `size` value returned from `emit_array_size`, which is the array's *total byte size* (base header size + len*elem_size), not the *count* of GC-reference elements. This `num_gc_refs` value is packed into the object's GC header (via `emit_gc_raw_alloc` -> `kind_and_reserved = kind | num_gc_refs`) and is later used by the DRC collector's tracing code to compute a slice of the object's outgoing GC-reference edges (count of `VMGcRef`-sized slots immediately following the header). Because `size` is numerically much larger than the true number of elements (and is a byte count rather than an element count), the collector believes the array has far more outgoing GC edges than it actually does. When tracing/dec-refing the array during collection, the GC walks past the end of the actual reference slots and off the end of the object/heap, reading and dec-refing arbitrary heap memory as if it were `VMGcRef` values. This is a heap buffer over-read (and consequent corruption of unrelated heap data via spurious ref-count decrements/frees) triggered simply by creating and then collecting a guest array-of-GC-refs value.
findings.suggestion: Use the array's element length (not its total byte size) when computing `num_gc_refs` for arrays whose elements are GC references. Refactor `emit_array_size` to take the already-computed `len` value instead of the `ArrayInit` (so the length can be reused), compute `len` once via `init.len(...)`, pass it into `emit_array_size`, and set `num_gc_refs = len` (the element count) instead of `num_gc_refs = size` (the byte size) when `array_layout.elems_are_gc_refs` is true.
findings.title: GC array of GC-refs reports byte size instead of element count as num_gc_refs

fix_commit.author: Nick Fitzgerald
fix_commit.message: Fix a bug where arrays of GC refs were misreporting their count of GC edges (#10453)

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: GC array of GC-refs reports byte size instead of element count as num_gc_refs

ground_truth.root_cause: The commit that introduced transitive dec-ref tracing in the DRC collector (#10401) added a new `num_gc_refs` header field used to bound the slice of outgoing GC edges traced during collection. For arrays of GC-ref elements, the author intended to pass the array length but accidentally reused the `size` local (the array's byte size in memory, computed by `emit_array_size`), since both were available in scope and the mistake (size vs. len) was an easy one given they are used adjacently. There was no type-level distinction between a 'byte size' ir::Value and an 'element count' ir::Value, so the compiler could not catch the mismatch.

pr_description:
* Transitively dec-ref objects in the DRC collector

Previously, the DRC collector only performed shallow reference counting where if
an object's ref count was decremented and reached zero, then we would deallocate
that object, but we would not decrement the reference counts of any other object
that was referenced by it. This commit changes that, so that now we will
decrement the reference counts of other objects referenced by an object that is
being deallocated.

This requires some method of tracing an object's outgoing edges. To avoid
needing to keep around and dispatch upon type-specific information about which
struct fields are GC references, for example, we instead pack all GC references
at the start of the object, just after its header. We additionally keep a count
of how many GC references an object has in its header. This allows us to create
a slice of any object's GC references, and we can uniformly trace any GC
object's outgoing edges. We don't need to reflect on the GC object's actual
type.

A final detail: the DRC collector was previously storing the object size in the
common GC header's reserved bits. It now stores the number of GC refs there
instead, and the object size is stored in its own field in the DRC-specific
header, next to the ref count. This is nice because, since we are making the DRC
header larger anyways, it raises the DRC collector's implementation limit on
object size from `u27::MAX` to `u32::MAX`.

Fixes #9701

* update disas tests

* Remove newly-added debug-assert that isn't true in certain edge cases

Sometimes we need to deallocate uninitialized objects when initializing their
fields fails, and this assertion trips.

* fix some tests by returning an error of the correct kind of trap

rather than a generic anyhow error

* fix tracing GC refs on big-endian architectures

We can't cast to a slice, we need to do conversion from little-endian bytes.

agent_reasoning: The struct.new/struct.new_default const-eval support added a fallible GC allocation path into `ConstExprEvaluator::eval`. The pre-existing global-initialization caller (`Instance::initialize_vmctx_globals`) was written before that allocation could fail, so it called `.expect("should be a valid const expr")` on the result, treating any evaluation failure as proof of an invalid module. A guest module with a struct-typed global initializer can legitimately hit this path and fail due to GC OOM/allocation failure at instantiation time, which would turn a recoverable condition into a host-side panic (embedder DoS). The fix changes `initialize_vmctx_globals` to return `Result<()>` and propagate the error with `?`, and wires that fallible call into the existing fallible instance post-initialization step so the error surfaces as a normal instantiation `Result::Err` instead of aborting the process.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 136500ed555e on top of intro a7e1150019bd via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): The wasi-nn host implementation's compute() function for HostGraphExecutionContext takes ownership of a Vec<NamedTensor> containing Resource<Tensor> handles supplied by the guest. Instead of removing (deleting) these resources from the host-side resource table once they are consumed, the code merely calls Table::get() to borrow/clone the tensor data, leaving the original table entries in place. Since the resource handles are consumed by value and never returned to the guest, the guest has no way to explicitly drop them either, so every call to compute() with input tensors permanently leaks one resource-table slot (and the backend memory referenced by it) per input tensor. Root cause: The refactor of the wasi-nn WIT bindings (commit a7e1150019) rewrote the compute() function to iterate `inputs.iter()` and fetch tensors via `self.table.get(&tensor_resource)` (a non-consuming borrow) rather than removing them from the table, despite the function taking ownership of the `Vec<NamedTensor>` (and thus the associated Resource handles) by value. This created a mismatch between resource ownership semantics (values fully consumed by the call) and the actual table cleanup performed (none), resulting in an unbounded resource-table growth / memory leak for every compute() invocation.

findings.message: In the HostGraphExecutionContext::compute implementation, the incoming `inputs: Vec<NamedTensor>` contains `Resource<Tensor>` handles that were previously pushed into `self.table` by the guest (via a resource-creating call such as load-tensor). The compute() function iterates the inputs with `inputs.iter()` and calls `self.table.get(&tensor_resopurce)` to obtain a cloned reference to the underlying tensor. `Table::get` only borrows/clones the entry; it never removes the resource from the host resource table. Because compute() consumes the `Resource<Tensor>` handles by value (the function signature takes `inputs: Vec<NamedTensor>`, not `&Vec<NamedTensor>`), the guest loses its only handle to these resources after the call returns, yet the resources are never deleted from the host table via `self.table.delete()`. This causes each compute() call to permanently leak one table slot (and the associated backend tensor data behind it) for every input tensor, since nothing else in the code path ever calls delete/drop on these resource handles.
findings.suggestion: Consume the input resources by iterating with `into_iter()` and remove each tensor resource from the table with `self.table.delete(tensor_resource)?` instead of merely borrowing it with `self.table.get(&tensor_resource)`. This releases the table slot (and any backend memory tied to it) once the tensor has been copied out for use in compute_with_io, matching the ownership semantics implied by consuming `inputs: Vec<NamedTensor>` by value.

agent_reasoning: Merged diff composed mechanically by cherry-picking fix 89fdfa12f718 on top of intro 1806c26562ec via git's 3-way merge. Vulnerability (LogicError): In the function `CompiledFunctionsTable::func_by_text_offset` (crates/environ/src/module_artifacts.rs), reverse-mapping a text-section PC offset to the owning `FuncKey` mishandles 'sparse' function-kind namespaces: it computes the sparse index as a namespace-local offset instead of converting it into the absolute index used by the shared `sparse_indices` table (by adding the namespace's `sparse_starts` base). This can produce a wrong `SparseIndex`, leading to incorrect function identification and, in builds with debug assertions / additional bounds checks downstream (e.g. `crates/environ/src/builtin.rs`), a reachable panic (`assertion failed: i < Self::len()`) triggerable via crafted Wasm modules that exercise this reverse lookup path (e.g. during traps/backtraces or GC/builtin trampoline resolution) with more than one sparse-kind function present. Root cause: The reverse PC->function lookup for sparse func-kind namespaces conflated a 'local offset within this namespace's slice of sparse index space' with the 'global/absolute SparseIndex' needed to index the single shared `sparse_indices` PrimaryMap across all namespaces. The per-namespace base offset (`sparse_starts[ns_idx]`) that the forward-building code (`CompiledFunctionsTableBuilder`) uses to lay out the sparse_indices table was never added back in on the lookup path.
commit_message:
Lookup functions in the text section by `FuncKey` at runtime (#11630)

This commit refactors our metadata, treating compiled functions homogeneously
and removing the need to add new tables to places like `CompiledModuleInfo`
whenever we add a new kind of function. This also simplifies the process of
constructing the metadata for a final, linked compilation artifact. Finally, it
paves the way to doing gc-sections during our linking process (which would give
us smaller code sizes by removing functions that have been inlined into every
caller, for example) as we now allow holes in certain types of function index
spaces that were previously always densely populated.

We have two kinds of index spaces:

1. Mostly-dense index spaces, which take O(max_index) space and provide O(1)
lookups.

2. Sparse index spaces, which take O(num_members) space and provide
O(log n) lookups.

Most of our function index spaces are currently dense, but we can tweak that in
the future if necessary.

Furthermore, code size of `.cwasm` binaries has shrunk very slightly with this
refactoring. Consider `spidermonkey.wasm`'s compiled `.cwasm`:

* Size before: 218756 `.wasmtime.info` section bytes, 20052632 total bytes
* Size after: 213761 `.wasmtime.info` section bytes, 20047640 total bytes

That is a 2.28% reduction on the size of the `.wasmtime.info` section, or a
0.025% reduction total.

However, we previously did a single metadata lookup to get the location of both
a Wasm function itself and its array-to-Wasm trampoline at the same time, and in
the new version of the code two lookups are performed. This is slightly slower,
as shown in our call-indirect micro-benchmark that combines lazy table
initialization (which delays looking up the function element's location until
runtime) with indirect-calling each table element exactly once (which defeats
the amortization of that lookup). So this micro-benchmark is both synthetic and
the worst-case scenario for this commit's change: we are measuring, as much as
we can, *only* the force-initialization-of-a-lazy-funcref-table-slot path.

Ultimately, I believe that the simplification is worth the regression in this
micro-benchmark.

Lookup functions in the text section by `FuncKey` at runtime (#11630)

This commit refactors our metadata, treating compiled functions homogeneously
and removing the need to add new tables to places like `CompiledModuleInfo`
whenever we add a new kind of function. This also simplifies the process of
constructing the metadata for a final, linked compilation artifact. Finally, it
paves the way to doing gc-sections during our linking process (which would give
us smaller code sizes by removing functions that have been inlined into every
caller, for example) as we now allow holes in certain types of function index
spaces that were previously always densely populated.

We have two kinds of index spaces:

1. Mostly-dense index spaces, which take O(max_index) space and provide O(1)
lookups.

2. Sparse index spaces, which take O(num_members) space and provide
O(log n) lookups.

Most of our function index spaces are currently dense, but we can tweak that in
the future if necessary.

Furthermore, code size of `.cwasm` binaries has shrunk very slightly with this
refactoring. Consider `spidermonkey.wasm`'s compiled `.cwasm`:

* Size before: 218756 `.wasmtime.info` section bytes, 20052632 total bytes
* Size after: 213761 `.wasmtime.info` section bytes, 20047640 total bytes

That is a 2.28% reduction on the size of the `.wasmtime.info` section, or a
0.025% reduction total.

However, we previously did a single metadata lookup to get the location of both
a Wasm function itself and its array-to-Wasm trampoline at the same time, and in
the new version of the code two lookups are performed. This is slightly slower,
as shown in our call-indirect micro-benchmark that combines lazy table
initialization (which delays looking up the function element's location until
runtime) with indirect-calling each table element exactly once (which defeats
the amortization of that lookup). So this micro-benchmark is both synthetic and
the worst-case scenario for this commit's change: we are measuring, as much as
we can, *only* the force-initialization-of-a-lazy-funcref-table-slot path.

Ultimately, I believe that the simplification is worth the regression in this
micro-benchmark.

findings.message: `CompiledFunctionsTable::func_by_text_offset` reverse-maps a text-section PC offset back to a `FuncKey`. For namespaces whose `FuncKeyKind` is 'sparse' (e.g. `ArrayToWasmTrampoline`, `WasmToBuiltinTrampoline`), the code computes `sparse_index` as simply `index.as_u32() - start.as_u32()` -- i.e. the offset of this function within the *namespace's local func_loc range* -- and uses that value directly as a `SparseIndex` to index into the table-wide `self.sparse_indices` map. However, `sparse_indices` is a single flat table shared across all namespaces, and each sparse namespace's entries begin at `self.sparse_starts[ns_idx]`, not at 0. The code never adds this per-namespace `sparse_start` offset before using the value as an absolute `SparseIndex`. As a result, for any namespace whose sparse segment does not begin at index 0 of `sparse_indices` (i.e. any sparse namespace after the first one), the computed `sparse_index` is wrong -- it is 'an offset within the kind's sparse index space' rather than the actual absolute `SparseIndex`. This produces either a wrong `FuncKey` being silently returned, or (further downstream, e.g. in `crates/environ/src/builtin.rs`'s `BuiltinFunctionIndex` / sparse-index backed assertions) an index value large enough to fail a `debug_assert!`/`assert!` bounds check such as `assert!(i < Self::len())`, causing a reachable panic / DoS triggerable from compiling and running attacker-controlled Wasm modules that exercise multiple sparse-kind functions (e.g. GC array operations combined with many Wasm functions, data/elem segment drops, etc., as in the reported reproducer).
findings.suggestion: When computing the sparse index for a non-dense (sparse) func-kind namespace, add the namespace's recorded `sparse_starts[ns_idx]` value to the locally-computed offset before converting it into a `SparseIndex`, so that the result is the correct absolute index into the shared `self.sparse_indices` table, matching how the forward/building logic in `CompiledFunctionsTableBuilder` lays entries out.

fix_commit.message: Fix reverse PC to function lookups for sparse func kinds (#11766)

must_cover.reason: Primary location of finding: Incorrect reverse PC-to-function lookup for sparse func kinds causes out-of-range index / panic

ground_truth.root_cause: The reverse PC->function lookup for sparse func-kind namespaces conflated a 'local offset within this namespace's slice of sparse index space' with the 'global/absolute SparseIndex' needed to index the single shared `sparse_indices` PrimaryMap across all namespaces. The per-namespace base offset (`sparse_starts[ns_idx]`) that the forward-building code (`CompiledFunctionsTableBuilder`) uses to lay out the sparse_indices table was never added back in on the lookup path.
